paras: The threat letter to J. T. Allen was an anonymous note left at the home of Allen, a Black Democrat in Cairo, Illinois, in August 1880, warning that he would be tarred, feathered and drummed out of town unless he left the Democratic clubs. No attack followed in the coverage, which comes only from the Democratic Cairo Bulletin, which printed the letter as evidence of Republican "bulldozing" during the campaign.

According to the Bulletin, Cairo's "colored Democrats" had faced insults and threats since declaring their politics, and had joined the Democratic Roosters' club and marched in its processions. Allen wrote that colored men had insulted him daily since the campaign opened and told him he would be "roughly handled" if he did not leave the party.

On the morning of Sunday, August 29, Allen found a letter on his front door step, which the Bulletin believed had been thrown there the night before. Addressed to him "and all other niger democrats," it ordered him to leave the Roosters or be "taired and fethered and drummed of of town," said he would never vote for Hancock and English, and was signed "Collored Republican." Allen took the letter to the Bulletin with a note declaring that threats would never scare him into the Republican ranks.

No investigation or arrest appears in the coverage. The rival Cairo News, as Allen quoted it, cast doubt on whether he had written what appeared under his name, and in a second letter on September 2 Allen insisted that he was the author and that the threat had been picked up at his door.

The Bulletin headlined the story "Republican Bulldozers," called the writers "cowards" and "Radicals," and asked readers of both parties whether such bulldozing should be tolerated. It called Allen a quiet man who avoided political talk and warned that the authors might themselves be "drummed out of town." No Black-press report of the threat was found.
The writer was never identified: Allen believed him a colored man, while the Bulletin judged from the disguised handwriting and phrases such as "take heed in time" that he was probably white.

accounts.label: Cairo Bulletin (Democratic)
accounts.gist: Republican 'bulldozers', angered that colored Democrats had joined the Roosters, sent Allen a threat; the Bulletin judged the writer probably a white man and warned the authors they would regret further attempts.

accounts.label: J. T. Allen
accounts.gist: He had been insulted and threatened daily by colored men since the campaign opened, then found the signed 'Colored Republican' letter at his door Sunday morning and printed it as written.

accounts.label: Cairo News (as quoted by Allen)
accounts.gist: Said Allen 'announces that he is the writer of the letter in yesterday's Bulletin' and, having only 'the general report to the contrary', gave him 'the benefit of his denial', implying doubt that Allen wrote what appeared under his name.

framing.detail: The Bulletin, a Democratic paper, headlined 'Republican Bulldozers' and called the writers 'cowards' and 'Radicals', using the threat as campaign material against the Republicans.

versions.value: Colored Republicans (Allen's opinion; the letter's signature)
Probably a white man, from the disguised handwriting and phrases such as 'take heed in time' (the Bulletin's view)

conflicts.note: Neither Allen nor the Bulletin claimed to know the writer; both are inferences.

versions.value: The Cairo News, as quoted by Allen, doubted that Allen wrote the letter printed over his name
Allen affirmed he wrote every article with his name and that the threat was picked up at his door

conflicts.note: The News is known only through Allen's quotation; which 'letter' it meant is not clear from the wording.
